newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish '96 registered trade gap seen $11 bln - min.
newsitem.headline: Polish '96 registered trade gap seen $11 bln - min.

text.p: Poland's registered trade gap counted by customs receipts, not current account flows, is expected to grow to $11 billion in 1996 against a $6.15 billion shortfall in 1995, an Economy Ministry analyst said on Monday.

Marian Zarzycki told Reuters official exports were likely to have grown by around eight percent last year, down from 32.8 percent growth in 1995, while imports increased by some 26 percent, also down from 1995's 34.7 percent growth.
"Slow economic growth in Germany and other EU countries, which constitute some 60 to 70 percent of Polish trade, cooled export growth rates last year," Zarzycki said.
"However, 1997 should be more optimistic as there are signals that economic growth in Western Europe will pick up again," he said, but did not give any forecasts.
He estimated unregistered cross-border trade revenue at around $5 billion last year, which would cut the actual trade deficit to around $6 billion.

The size of cross-border trade, mainly carried out by Germans and Russians buying food or petrol in Poland, is an estimate made by the central bank on the basis of currency purchases in exchange bureaux.
However the expected $11 billion denotes the gap in official trade conducted by companies which pay taxes and are affected by macro-economic policy moves.
The Central Statistical Office (GUS) said registered trade figures for the first three quarters of 1996, counted by customs receipts, should be available by the end of January.
The central bank, which counts trade by current account flows, said Poland had a $6.4 billion merchandise trade deficit during the January-October period of 1996.
The bank said Poland's current account deficit during that period, including cross border trade revenue, was $860 million. It is due to release current account data for 1996 in February.

The customs receipts declare the amount and value of goods that cross the border. The figure differs from current account data mainly because of the time lag between when the goods cross the border and the transfer of cash being made.
